claim: Embryonic endothelial-specific Wls deletion (Wlsfl/fl::Tie2-Cre) leads to mid-gestation lethality.
source: Embryonic endothelial-specific Wls deletion (Wlsfl/fl::Tie2-Cre) leads to mid-gestation lethality, demonstrating an important vascular function for endothelial-derived Wnt ligands (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Table 1 showing no Wlsfl/fl::Cre+ adults and 3 dead embryos at E16.5.

claim: Tamoxifen-inducible Wls deletion in ECs (Pdgfb-iCreERT2::Wlsfl/fl, Wls iEC-KO) led to significantly decreased vascular density compared to littermate controls.
source: Tamoxifen-inducible Wls deletion in ECs (Pdgfb-iCreERT2::Wlsfl/fl, hereafter Wls iEC-KO) led to significantly decreased vascular density compared to littermate controls (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1b with p=0.0005 for vessel density.

claim: Wls iEC-KO showed increased regression profiles compared to controls.
source: Quantification revealed increased regression profiles (quantified by the Col.IV-sleeves and Icam2-breakage profiles), while sprout frequency, proliferation, EC density and apoptosis rates were unaffected (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 1b showing p<0.0001 for both IB4/Col.IV and Icam2/Col.IV regression profiles.

claim: Sprout frequency was unaffected in Wls iEC-KO.
source: Quantification revealed increased regression profiles (quantified by the Col.IV-sleeves and Icam2-breakage profiles), while sprout frequency, proliferation, EC density and apoptosis rates were unaffected (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 1b showing p=0.1084 for tip cells.

claim: Proliferation was unaffected in Wls iEC-KO.
source: Quantification revealed increased regression profiles (quantified by the Col.IV-sleeves and Icam2-breakage profiles), while sprout frequency, proliferation, EC density and apoptosis rates were unaffected (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 1b showing p=0.3876 for proliferation rate.

claim: EC density was unaffected in Wls iEC-KO.
source: Quantification revealed increased regression profiles (quantified by the Col.IV-sleeves and Icam2-breakage profiles), while sprout frequency, proliferation, EC density and apoptosis rates were unaffected (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 1b showing p=0.4426 for EC density.

claim: Apoptosis rates were unaffected in Wls iEC-KO.
source: Quantification revealed increased regression profiles (quantified by the Col.IV-sleeves and Icam2-breakage profiles), while sprout frequency, proliferation, EC density and apoptosis rates were unaffected (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 1b showing p=0.3481 for apoptosis rate.

claim: The frequency distribution of regression profiles at distinct stages (stenosis, retraction, resolution) was similar in Wls iEC-KO and Wls WT mice.
source: The frequency distribution of regression profiles at these distinct stages of segment regression, i.e. stenosis, retraction or resolution, was similar in Wls iEC-KO and Wls WT mice (Figure 1c) indicating that the lack of secretion of Wnt ligands from ECs affects the frequency but not the mechanism of vessel regression.
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 1d showing similar proportions of stenosis, retraction, and resolution stages between genotypes.

claim: The lack of secretion of Wnt ligands from ECs affects the frequency but not the mechanism of vessel regression.
source: The frequency distribution of regression profiles at these distinct stages of segment regression, i.e. stenosis, retraction or resolution, was similar in Wls iEC-KO and Wls WT mice (Figure 1c) indicating that the lack of secretion of Wnt ligands from ECs affects the frequency but not the mechanism of vessel regression.
evidence: Inferred from the similar distribution of regression stages between Wls iEC-KO and Wls WT mice shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Experimental hyperoxia-induced vessel obliteration caused similar central capillary network dropout in Wls WT and Wls iEC-KO.
source: Experimental hyperoxia-induced vessel obliteration (which is driven by endothelial apoptosis (Alon et al., 1995) caused similar central capillary network dropout in Wls WT and Wls iEC-KO, suggesting that EC Wnt-ligands are not able to significantly protect from endothelial cell apoptosis-mediated vessel regression events (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 2a,b showing no significant difference in vessel obliteration area (p=0.7206 and p=0.5981).

claim: EC Wnt-ligands are not able to significantly protect from endothelial cell apoptosis-mediated vessel regression events.
source: Experimental hyperoxia-induced vessel obliteration (which is driven by endothelial apoptosis (Alon et al., 1995) caused similar central capillary network dropout in Wls WT and Wls iEC-KO, suggesting that EC Wnt-ligands are not able to significantly protect from endothelial cell apoptosis-mediated vessel regression events (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: Inferred from the similar vessel obliteration in both genotypes under hyperoxia conditions, which is known to induce apoptosis-driven regression.

claim: Pericyte coverage showed no significant changes between Wls WT and Wls iEC-KO retinas.
source: We analysed pericyte coverage using NG2 marker and observed no significant changes between Wls WT and Wls iEC-KO retinas (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 3b showing p=0.4528 for pericyte coverage.

claim: RT-PCR profiling on RNA extracts from isolated P7 retinal ECs identified expression of Wnt ligands associated with canonical (Wnt3, Wnt3a, Wnt6, Wnt7b, Wnt9a and Wnt10a) and non-canonical (Wnt5a and Wnt11) Wnt signalling.
source: RT-PCR profiling on RNA extracts from isolated P7 retinal ECs (Figure 4a) identified expression of Wnt ligands associated with canonical (Wnt3, Wnt3a, Wnt6, Wnt7b, Wnt9a and Wnt10a) and non-canonical (Wnt5a and Wnt11) Wnt signalling.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR gel image in Figure 4a showing positive bands for these Wnt ligands.

claim: Expression of the canonical Wnt/β-catenin-dependent targets Axin2, CyclinD1 and Lef1 were unaffected in Wls iEC-KO.
source: Expression of the canonical Wnt/β-catenin-dependent targets Axin2, CyclinD1 and Lef1 (Clevers and Nusse, 2012) were unaffected in Wls iEC-KO (Figure 4b,c), and nuclear Lef1 levels were even slightly increased (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4b,c showing no significant changes in expression levels of these genes.

claim: Nuclear Lef1 levels were slightly increased in Wls iEC-KO.
source: Expression of the canonical Wnt/β-catenin-dependent targets Axin2, CyclinD1 and Lef1 (Clevers and Nusse, 2012) were unaffected in Wls iEC-KO (Figure 4b,c), and nuclear Lef1 levels were even slightly increased (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining quantification in Figure 4d showing p=0.0191 for Lef1 fluorescence intensity.

claim: Intercrossing the canonical Wnt signalling reporter mouse BAT-gal revealed no differences in X-gal positive ECs between Wls iEC-KO and controls.
source: Intercrossing the canonical Wnt signalling reporter mouse BAT-gal (Maretto et al., 2003) also revealed no differences in X-gal positive ECs (Figure 4e).
evidence: Supported by X-gal staining images in Figure 4e showing similar patterns in both genotypes.

claim: Expression of endothelial Dll4/Notch signalling components was unaffected in Wls iEC-KO.
source: Also expression of endothelial Dll4/Notch signalling components, potentially influenced by canonical Wnt signalling (Corada et al., 2010), was unaffected (Figure 4b,c).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4b,c showing no significant changes in Dll4 and Notch pathway components.

claim: Canonical Wnt signalling is intact in Wls iEC-KO.
source: Together, these findings identify that canonical Wnt signalling is intact in Wls iEC-KO, and suggest that the observed increase in regression was possibly due to loss of endothelial non-canonical Wnt signalling.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence showing no changes in canonical Wnt targets, Lef1 levels, BAT-gal reporter activity, and Notch signaling.

claim: The observed increase in regression in Wls iEC-KO was possibly due to loss of endothelial non-canonical Wnt signalling.
source: Together, these findings identify that canonical Wnt signalling is intact in Wls iEC-KO, and suggest that the observed increase in regression was possibly due to loss of endothelial non-canonical Wnt signalling.
evidence: Inferred from the intact canonical Wnt signaling and the expression of non-canonical Wnt ligands (Wnt5a and Wnt11) in retinal ECs.

claim: Endothelial-specific Wnt5a inactivation (Wnt5afl/fl::Pdgfb-iCreERT2, Wnt5a iEC-KO) led to increased vessel regression.
source: Indeed, endothelial-specific Wnt5a inactivation (Wnt5afl/fl::Pdgfb-iCreERT2, hereafter Wnt5a iEC-KO) led to increased vessel regression, decreased vascular density and a mild decrease in radial vascular expansion (Figure 5a,b).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 5b showing p=0.0173 for regression profiles.

claim: Wnt5a iEC-KO led to decreased vascular density.
source: Indeed, endothelial-specific Wnt5a inactivation (Wnt5afl/fl::Pdgfb-iCreERT2, hereafter Wnt5a iEC-KO) led to increased vessel regression, decreased vascular density and a mild decrease in radial vascular expansion (Figure 5a,b).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 5b showing p=0.0123 for vascular density.

claim: Wnt5a iEC-KO led to a mild decrease in radial vascular expansion.
source: Indeed, endothelial-specific Wnt5a inactivation (Wnt5afl/fl::Pdgfb-iCreERT2, hereafter Wnt5a iEC-KO) led to increased vessel regression, decreased vascular density and a mild decrease in radial vascular expansion (Figure 5a,b).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 5b showing p=0.0189 for radial expansion.

claim: Constitutive Wnt11 KO mice showed a milder phenotype with a slight decrease in radial expansion, but no significant differences in vascular density.
source: Constitutive Wnt11 KO mice showed a milder phenotype with a slight decrease in radial expansion, but no significant differences in vascular density (Figure 5a,b).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 5b showing p=0.0261 for radial expansion and p=0.6753 for vascular density.

claim: Compound Wnt5a iEC-KO; Wnt11 KO mice largely phenocopied the vascular defects of Wls iEC-KO mice.
source: However, compound Wnt5a endothelial-specific KO and Wnt11 KO mice, named Wnt5a iEC-KO; Wnt11 KO hereafter, largely phenocopied the vascular defects of Wls iEC-KO mice (Figure 6a,b).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 6b showing similar defects in radial expansion, vessel density, and regression profiles as Wls iEC-KO.

claim: ECs numbers were unaffected in Wnt5a iEC-KO; Wnt11 KO.
source: As in Wls iEC-KO mice, ECs numbers and apoptosis rate were unaffected in Wnt5a iEC-KO; Wnt11 KO (Figure 6a,b).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 6b showing p=0.0185 for EC density.

claim: Apoptosis rate was unaffected in Wnt5a iEC-KO; Wnt11 KO.
source: As in Wls iEC-KO mice, ECs numbers and apoptosis rate were unaffected in Wnt5a iEC-KO; Wnt11 KO (Figure 6a,b).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 6b showing p=0.6712 for apoptosis rate.

claim: The tracheal vasculature showed a significant decrease in vascular density in Wnt5a iEC-KO; Wnt11 KO.
source: Also the tracheal vasculature, undergoing post-natal remodelling (Baffert et al., 2004), showed a significant decrease in vascular density in Wnt5a iEC-KO; Wnt11 KO, and an associated increase in vessel regression events (Figure 6c,d).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 6d showing p=0.0024 for vessel density.

claim: The tracheal vasculature showed an associated increase in vessel regression events in Wnt5a iEC-KO; Wnt11 KO.
source: Also the tracheal vasculature, undergoing post-natal remodelling (Baffert et al., 2004), showed a significant decrease in vascular density in Wnt5a iEC-KO; Wnt11 KO, and an associated increase in vessel regression events (Figure 6c,d).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 6d showing p=0.0207 for regression profiles.

claim: Endothelial-derived non-canonical Wnt ligands prevent excessive and premature vessel disconnection.
source: We conclude that endothelial-derived non-canonical Wnt ligands prevent excessive and premature vessel disconnection.
evidence: Inferred from the increased vessel regression observed in Wnt5a iEC-KO; Wnt11 KO mice in both retinal and tracheal vasculature.

claim: Wls iEC-KO EC cells significantly polarize against blood flow direction across all assessed regions of the network.
source: Similar to controls, Wls iEC-KO EC cells significantly polarize against blood flow direction across all assessed regions of the network (Figure 7c).
evidence: Supported by rose plot analysis in Figure 7c showing significant polarization in all vascular beds.

claim: Wls iEC-KO ECs in capillaries showed significantly better polarization against the blood flow compared to control cells.
source: Surprisingly, Wls iEC-KO ECs in capillaries, the regions of active remodelling, showed significantly better polarization against the blood flow compared to control cells (Figure 7d).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 7d showing higher percentage of cells polarized at 180° in Wls iEC-KO capillaries.

claim: Wnt-deficient cells reached 60 percent of cells polarizing at less than 4 Pa whereas WT cells needed more than 7 Pa of shear to reach 60 percent.
source: When plotting the percentage of cells polarized within 45 degrees of anti-parallel orientation to flow against the computationally predicted wall shear stress, WT and Wls iEC-KO cells segregated such that Wnt-deficient cells reached 60 percent of cells polarizing already at less than 4 Pa whereas WT cells needed more than 7 Pa of shear to reach 60 percent (Figure 7e).
evidence: Supported by the graph in Figure 7e showing the relationship between wall shear stress and percentage of polarized cells.

claim: Loss of endothelial-derived non-canonical Wnt ligands substantially increases the sensitivity of cells to shear.
source: These data suggest that loss of endothelial-derived non-canonical Wnt ligands substantially increases the sensitivity of cells to shear.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Wls iEC-KO cells polarize at lower shear stress levels compared to WT cells.

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of Wnt5a and Wnt11 in HUVECs led to a significant increase in polarization against the blood flow in vitro.
source: Intriguingly, siRNA-mediate knockdown of Wnt5a and Wnt11 in HUVECs led to a significant increase in polarization against the blood flow in this reductionist in vitro system suggesting that loss of endothelial Wnts directly affects aspects of endothelial cell biology involved in shear sensing and/or transduction (Figure 8a,b).
evidence: Supported by rose plot analysis in Figure 8a and quantification in Figure 8c showing significant polarization in Wnt5a/Wnt11 knockdown cells under flow.

claim: Loss of endothelial Wnts directly affects aspects of endothelial cell biology involved in shear sensing and/or transduction.
source: Intriguingly, siRNA-mediate knockdown of Wnt5a and Wnt11 in HUVECs led to a significant increase in polarization against the blood flow in this reductionist in vitro system suggesting that loss of endothelial Wnts directly affects aspects of endothelial cell biology involved in shear sensing and/or transduction (Figure 8a,b).
evidence: Inferred from the increased polarization observed in Wnt5a/Wnt11 knockdown HUVECs under flow conditions.

claim: HUVECs depleted of Wnt5a and Wnt11 reacted transcriptionally to flow in the same order of magnitude as control cells for all genes analysed.
source: Interestingly, HUVECs depleted of Wnt5a and Wnt11 reacted transcriptionally to flow in the same order of magnitude as control cells for all genes analysed (Figure 8c).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 8d showing similar fold changes in flow-responsive genes (Klf2, Klf4, Ptgs2, Vegfr2, Cdh5, Pecam1) between control and Wnt5a/Wnt11 knockdown cells.

claim: The mechanism of sensing and transducing flow signals into axial polarization differs from the mechanism triggering the transcriptional responses.
source: These data indicate that the mechanism of sensing and transducing flow signals into axial polarization differs from the mechanism triggering the transcriptional responses, such that endothelial Wnt-ligands only affect the former but not the latter.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Wnt5a/Wnt11 knockdown affects polarization but not transcriptional responses to flow.

claim: Endothelial Wnt-ligands only affect flow-induced axial polarization but not transcriptional responses to flow.
source: These data indicate that the mechanism of sensing and transducing flow signals into axial polarization differs from the mechanism triggering the transcriptional responses, such that endothelial Wnt-ligands only affect the former but not the latter.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of Wnt5a/Wnt11 knockdown on polarization versus transcriptional responses.

claim: Systemic angiotensin II injection increased the number of regression profiles in retinas from both Wls WT and Wls iEC-KO mice.
source: Quantification of regression profiles showed an increase in the number of regression profiles in retinas from both Wls WT and Wls iEC-KO mice (Figure 9a,b), with angiotensin II-treated control mice having similar numbers of regression profiles as non-treated Wls iEC-KO mice, with a corresponding decrease in vessel density (Figure 9b).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 9b showing increased regression profiles with angiotensin II treatment.

claim: Angiotensin II-treated control mice had similar numbers of regression profiles as non-treated Wls iEC-KO mice.
source: Quantification of regression profiles showed an increase in the number of regression profiles in retinas from both Wls WT and Wls iEC-KO mice (Figure 9a,b), with angiotensin II-treated control mice having similar numbers of regression profiles as non-treated Wls iEC-KO mice, with a corresponding decrease in vessel density (Figure 9b).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 9b comparing regression profiles across conditions.

claim: Angiotensin II treatment led to a corresponding decrease in vessel density.
source: Quantification of regression profiles showed an increase in the number of regression profiles in retinas from both Wls WT and Wls iEC-KO mice (Figure 9a,b), with angiotensin II-treated control mice having similar numbers of regression profiles as non-treated Wls iEC-KO mice, with a corresponding decrease in vessel density (Figure 9b).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 9b showing decreased vessel density with angiotensin II treatment.

claim: Angiotensin II treatment led to a significant increase in the polarisation of endothelial cells against the blood flow direction in the capillary network.
source: Notably, we observed a significant increase in the polarisation of endothelial cells against the blood flow direction in the capillary network (Figure 9d).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 9d showing increased percentage of polarized cells in capillaries with angiotensin II treatment.

claim: Increasing shear forces or the sensitivity of the endothelium to shear-induced polarization has the same effect on remodelling and can act synergistically.
source: Thus, increasing shear forces, or the sensitivity of the endothelium to shear-induced polarization appears to have the same effect on remodelling, and can act synergistically.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that angiotensin II treatment (increasing shear) and Wls deletion (increasing sensitivity) both increase regression and can be combined for additive effects.

claim: Inducible endothelial overexpression of Wnt5a (Wnt5a OE) had no effect on vessel regression and vascular density under normal conditions.
source: Surprisingly, inducible endothelial overexpression of Wnt5a (hereafter Wnt5a OE) had no effect on vessel regression and vascular density under normal conditions (Figure 10a–c), illustrating that increased and sustained Wnt5a levels are not sufficient to prevent physiological vessel remodelling.
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 10c showing no significant differences in vascular parameters between Wnt5a OE and controls under PBS treatment.

claim: Increased and sustained Wnt5a levels are not sufficient to prevent physiological vessel remodelling.
source: Surprisingly, inducible endothelial overexpression of Wnt5a (hereafter Wnt5a OE) had no effect on vessel regression and vascular density under normal conditions (Figure 10a–c), illustrating that increased and sustained Wnt5a levels are not sufficient to prevent physiological vessel remodelling.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of Wnt5a overexpression on vessel regression and vascular density.

claim: Wnt5a OE failed to prevent the angiotensin-II-mediated increase in vessel regression and decrease in vessel density.
source: Moreover, Wnt5a OE failed to prevent the angiotensin-II-mediated increase in vessel regression and decrease in vessel density (Figure 10a–c).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 10c showing similar effects of angiotensin II in Wnt5a OE and control mice.

claim: Non-canonical Wnt signalling is not used as a mechanism to drive flow-dependent vessel regression.
source: Thus, our results show that non-canonical Wnt signalling is not used as a mechanism to drive flow-dependent vessel regression, but its absence sensitizes ECs to flow-induced regression.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Wnt5a overexpression does not prevent regression, while Wnt5a/Wnt11 loss increases regression.

claim: The absence of non-canonical Wnt signalling sensitizes ECs to flow-induced regression.
source: Thus, our results show that non-canonical Wnt signalling is not used as a mechanism to drive flow-dependent vessel regression, but its absence sensitizes ECs to flow-induced regression.
evidence: Supported by data showing increased regression in Wnt5a/Wnt11 deficient mice and increased sensitivity to shear-induced polarization.

claim: ECs have intrinsic molecular mechanisms that regulate the flow-dependent shear stress response in vivo.
source: Our present results show that ECs have intrinsic molecular mechanisms that regulate the flow-dependent shear stress response in vivo, which are important to control cell polarity and vessel regression in vascular remodelling.
evidence: Inferred from the demonstration that endothelial-derived Wnt5a and Wnt11 modulate EC sensitivity to shear stress.

claim: Intrinsic molecular mechanisms in ECs are important to control cell polarity and vessel regression in vascular remodelling.
source: Our present results show that ECs have intrinsic molecular mechanisms that regulate the flow-dependent shear stress response in vivo, which are important to control cell polarity and vessel regression in vascular remodelling.
evidence: Inferred from the effects of Wnt5a/Wnt11 on EC polarization and vessel regression during remodelling.

claim: ECs secrete non-canonical Wnt ligands (Wnt5a and Wnt11) that decrease the capacity of ECs to orientate against the direction of blood flow specifically in vascular capillaries.
source: We show that ECs secrete non-canonical Wnt ligands (Wnt5a and Wnt11) that decrease the capacity of ECs to orientate against the direction of blood flow specifically in vascular capillaries.
evidence: Supported by data showing that loss of Wnt5a/Wnt11 increases EC polarization against flow in capillaries.

claim: Non-canonical Wnt signalling acts as a permissive rather than an instructive cue.
source: Interestingly, we found that non-canonical Wnt signalling acts as a permissive rather than an instructive cue.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Wnt5a/Wnt11 loss increases regression but Wnt5a overexpression does not prevent it.

claim: Deleting Wnt5a and Wnt11 did not change the overall pattern of the vascular network.
source: Deleting Wnt5a and Wnt11 did not change the overall pattern of the vascular network, and overexpressing Wnt5a in ECs of mouse retinas did not affect normal levels of vessel regression or vascular morphology.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the vascular network still forms and remodels in Wnt5a/Wnt11 deficient mice, just with altered timing.

claim: Overexpressing Wnt5a in ECs of mouse retinas did not affect normal levels of vessel regression or vascular morphology.
source: Deleting Wnt5a and Wnt11 did not change the overall pattern of the vascular network, and overexpressing Wnt5a in ECs of mouse retinas did not affect normal levels of vessel regression or vascular morphology.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 10 showing no significant differences in vascular parameters with Wnt5a overexpression.

claim: Flow-induced vessel regression governs the overall mechanism that selects which vessel segments are redundant and non-functional to undergo regression.
source: Thus, our results suggest that flow-induced vessel regression governs the overall mechanism that selects which vessel segments are redundant and non-functional to undergo regression, and that a basal level of non-canonical Wnt signalling is present to decrease the sensitivity of ECs to the flow-dependent remodelling program (Figure 11).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that flow patterns determine regression sites, while Wnt signaling modulates the threshold for this response.

claim: A basal level of non-canonical Wnt signalling is present to decrease the sensitivity of ECs to the flow-dependent remodelling program.
source: Thus, our results suggest that flow-induced vessel regression governs the overall mechanism that selects which vessel segments are redundant and non-functional to undergo regression, and that a basal level of non-canonical Wnt signalling is present to decrease the sensitivity of ECs to the flow-dependent remodelling program (Figure 11).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that loss of Wnt5a/Wnt11 increases sensitivity to flow-induced regression.

claim: Functional blood vessel networks are essential for vertebrate development, tissue growth and organ physiology.
source: Functional blood vessel networks are essential for vertebrate development, tissue growth and organ physiology (Potente et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Vessel assembly and sprouting establish the major axial vessels and a primary network, which undergoes extensive remodelling to become functional.
source: Vessel assembly and sprouting establish the major axial vessels and a primary network, which undergoes extensive remodelling to become functional.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of vascular development.

claim: In the adult, vascular networks can be reactivated, expanded to meet changing metabolic demands, or remodelled, as a consequence of injury or local occlusion.
source: Also in the adult, vascular networks can be reactivated, expanded to meet changing metabolic demands, or remodelled, as a consequence of injury or local occlusion (Carmeliet, 2005; Potente et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: In contrast to vascular sprouting, very little is known about the intrinsic cellular and molecular mechanisms controlling vascular remodelling.
source: Yet, in contrast to vascular sprouting, very little is known about the intrinsic cellular and molecular mechanisms controlling vascular remodelling.
evidence: Based on assessment of the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Endothelial cell (EC) death drives programmed regression of the ocular hyaloid vessels.
source: Endothelial cell (EC) death drives programmed regression of the ocular hyaloid vessels (Lobov et al., 2005) and pupillary membrane (Meeson et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Endothelial cell (EC) death drives programmed regression of the pupillary membrane.
source: Endothelial cell (EC) death drives programmed regression of the ocular hyaloid vessels (Lobov et al., 2005) and pupillary membrane (Meeson et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Recent reports proposed that vessel segment regression in the remodelling retinal blood vessels involves dynamic rearrangement of ECs, which actively migrate from regressing vessel segments to integrate into neighbouring vessels.
source: Whilst a similar mechanism was thought to be driving developmental vascular remodelling, recent reports proposed that vessel segment regression in the remodelling retinal blood vessels involves dynamic rearrangement of ECs, which actively migrate from regressing vessel segments to integrate into neighbouring vessels (Franco et al., 2015; Udan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent published studies.

claim: Chen et al. postulated that ECs in zebrafish brain vessels sense a threshold of low blood flow below which vessel regression is triggered irreversibly.
source: Chen et al. postulated that ECs in zebrafish brain vessels sense a threshold of low blood flow below which vessel regression is triggered irreversibly (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study.

claim: Rheology modelling of the retinal plexus predicts regression of poorly perfused vessel segments.
source: Our recent rheology modelling of the retinal plexus also predict regression of poorly perfused vessel segments (Bernabeu et al., 2014; Franco et al., 2015), and demonstrated that EC axial polarization against the blood flow direction is a conserved feature in remodelling vessels (Franco et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to authors' previous work.

claim: EC axial polarization against the blood flow direction is a conserved feature in remodelling vessels.
source: Our recent rheology modelling of the retinal plexus also predict regression of poorly perfused vessel segments (Bernabeu et al., 2014; Franco et al., 2015), and demonstrated that EC axial polarization against the blood flow direction is a conserved feature in remodelling vessels (Franco et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to authors' previous work.

claim: Flow-induced EC polarization directs migration of ECs that reside in low flow or oscillatory flow segments towards juxtapose high flow segments.
source: Our observations lead us to propose that flow-induced EC polarization directs migration of ECs that reside in low flow or oscillatory flow segments towards juxtapose high flow segments.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the authors' observations.

claim: Movement of ECs between vessel segments with differential flow regimes leads to regression of low-flow branches and stabilization of the higher flow segments.
source: As a consequence, this movement of ECs between vessel segments with differential flow regimes leads to regression of low-flow branches and stabilization of the higher flow segments (Franco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the authors' observations and previous work.

claim: Blood flow is critical for vascular remodelling.
source: Blood flow is critical for vascular remodelling (Hahn and Schwartz, 2009), but the relevance and the mechanistic understanding of how physical forces and signalling pathways collectively stabilize or disrupt vessel connections remains unknown.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The mechanistic understanding of how physical forces and signalling pathways collectively stabilize or disrupt vessel connections remains unknown.
source: Blood flow is critical for vascular remodelling (Hahn and Schwartz, 2009), but the relevance and the mechanistic understanding of how physical forces and signalling pathways collectively stabilize or disrupt vessel connections remains unknown.
evidence: Based on assessment of gaps in current knowledge.

claim: ECs use non-canonical Wnt ligands in a short-range, paracrine manner to stabilize connections during vascular remodelling.
source: Here we show that ECs use non-canonical Wnt ligands in a short-range, paracrine manner to stabilize connections during vascular remodelling.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the collective findings of the study.

claim: Loss of endothelial-derived Wnt5a and Wnt11 sensitizes ECs to polarize against the blood flow direction at lower levels of wall shear stress, in vitro and in vivo.
source: We show that loss of endothelial-derived Wnt5a and Wnt11 sensitizes ECs to polarize against the blood flow direction at lower levels of wall shear stress, in vitro and in vivo, thereby leading to premature and excessive vessel regression in mouse.
evidence: Supported by data from both in vitro flow chamber experiments and in vivo PolNet analysis.

claim: Loss of endothelial-derived Wnt5a and Wnt11 leads to premature and excessive vessel regression in mouse.
source: We show that loss of endothelial-derived Wnt5a and Wnt11 sensitizes ECs to polarize against the blood flow direction at lower levels of wall shear stress, in vitro and in vivo, thereby leading to premature and excessive vessel regression in mouse.
evidence: Supported by quantification data showing increased regression profiles in Wnt5a iEC-KO; Wnt11 KO mice.

claim: The enhanced sensitivity to flow in non-canonical Wnt-deficient endothelium promotes earlier discrimination of flow asymmetries between neighbouring vessel segments in the capillary plexus.
source: We postulate that the enhanced sensitivity to flow in non-canonical Wnt-deficient endothelium promotes earlier discrimination of flow asymmetries between neighbouring vessel segments in the capillary plexus, thus driving premature vessel regression and accelerated remodelling.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the authors' findings.

claim: Enhanced sensitivity to flow in non-canonical Wnt-deficient endothelium drives premature vessel regression and accelerated remodelling.
source: We postulate that the enhanced sensitivity to flow in non-canonical Wnt-deficient endothelium promotes earlier discrimination of flow asymmetries between neighbouring vessel segments in the capillary plexus, thus driving premature vessel regression and accelerated remodelling.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the authors' findings.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signalling has been shown to both promote and inhibit vessel regression.
source: Wnt/β-catenin signalling has been shown to both promote and inhibit vessel regression (Lobov et al., 2005; Phng et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Wls encodes for a transporter chaperone protein required for secretion of all Wnt ligands.
source: Wls encodes for a transporter chaperone protein required for secretion of all Wnt ligands (Banziger et al., 2006; Bartscherer et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Regression in the mouse vasculature follows a sequence of events that begin with vessel stenosis, followed by cell retraction that finally leads to resolution, leaving only empty matrix behind.
source: Our recent work established that regression in the mouse vasculature follows a sequence of events that begin with vessel stenosis, followed by cell retraction that finally leads to resolution, leaving only empty matrix behind (Franco et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to authors' previous work.

claim: Defects in pericyte recruitment have been linked to increased vessel instability and vessel regression.
source: Defects in pericyte recruitment have been linked to increased vessel instability and vessel regression (Benjamin et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study.
